faqs.q: What does wildlife removal cost in Mount Holly?
faqs.a: Pricing turns on the species involved, the height and condition of the roofline, and whether droppings or nesting debris need cleaning out afterward. Mount Holly's older masonry and layered additions widen the range between a simple job and a big one, which is why the inspection here spends extra time on the seams between building eras. Every job starts with an inspection; you get the full figure in writing before removal or sealing begins, and nothing is quoted sight-unseen over the phone.

faqs.q: Can bats be evicted from my Mount Holly attic in the summer?
faqs.a: Not in midsummer. NJ Fish & Wildlife guidelines limit bat evictions to April 1 through May 14 and August 1 through October 15, because flightless pups would be trapped inside during the May 15 to July 31 maternity stretch. The creek-side Victorians in Mount Holly hold the town's summer colonies, and their owners usually call in June, mid-maternity season, when the honest answer is a survey now and exclusion booked for the August window. The work is exclusion only: one-way exits fitted during an open window, left in place through several mild nights, then every gap sealed once the colony has left. Bats are never trapped or killed — they are protected under the state's Endangered and Nongame Species Conservation Act.

Mount Holly.wildlife_intro:
Mount Holly is a working county seat of brick rowhouses, Victorian twins, and frame homes stacked between Rancocas Creek and the hill the town is named for. Mill Race Village and the old High Street blocks carry two centuries of alterations, and the seams between additions are where animals get in. Raccoons den in the older chimneys, bats work the tall attics along the creek, and rats thread the old commercial basements downtown. Out on the Route 38 side, postwar streets add the standard squirrel-and-soffit rotation.

Attached housing changes the math. In a rowhouse or twin, one animal in a shared attic or party-wall void is every neighbor's problem, and sealing a single unit while the adjoining roofline stays open just moves the tenant sideways. We inspect the whole run of connected rooflines where access allows, coordinate timing with neighbors when entries cross property lines, and seal the full set of openings under one plan. Older masonry party walls hide voids that let squirrels travel between houses unseen — finding those routes is most of the job in attached stock. Mount Holly's attached and semi-attached stock means entries often sit on a shared roofline, and the sealing plan here covers the whole seam, not one owner's slice of it.

faqs.q: Why do I hear running in my Marlton ceiling every morning?
faqs.a: Daytime running, especially at dawn and mid-afternoon, points to gray squirrels — they commute. In Kings Grant and Woodstream the morning running usually starts at a corner soffit the squirrels reached from the canopy, and the neighboring houses often share the same failing detail. A squirrel entry is usually a gnawed widening at a gable vent, dormer cheek, or eave return, and the repair has to replace the chewed wood and back it with metal, or the next squirrel reopens it in days. One-way doors let the animals leave on their own schedule; then the opening is closed for good.

faqs.q: Moles are tearing up my Marlton yard — how are they handled?
faqs.a: By trapping the active runs, not by poison peanuts or vibrating stakes, which mostly rearrange the damage. Surface ridges are feeding tunnels; the deep runs along edges and foundations are the travel lanes where traps belong. Marlton's irrigated subdivision lawns are grub-rich and soft, which is why mole ridging here shows up in neat street-by-street clusters after wet springs. Eastern moles work most New Jersey lawns, and the star-nosed mole turns up in wetter ground. Expect a few visits spaced out — mole work is verified by fresh ridging stopping, not by a single day's catch.

Marlton.wildlife_intro:
Marlton is the village heart of Evesham Township: big postwar and 1970s subdivisions like Kings Grant and Woodstream, newer construction around the Greentree Road corridor, and a mature pine-and-oak canopy over nearly all of it. The calls are suburban classics with a local twist. Squirrels and raccoons work the soffits of the Kings Grant colonials, groundhogs dig under the sheds of the larger Woodstream lots, and the wooded edges toward Medford and the Rancocas headwaters send skunks and opossums into crawlspaces all year.

Most entries are not holes animals made — they are building failures animals found. Fascia boards rot behind gutters, soffit panels sag at the seams, and a gray squirrel needs only a small gap and one afternoon to widen it. Repairs here mean replacing the rotted wood, not just covering it, then backing vents and eave returns with metal that teeth cannot work through. Paint-matched covers keep the fix invisible from the street. Gutters clogged with leaf litter matter too: standing water softens the very boards that are supposed to keep animals out. In Marlton the recurring failure is the soffit line on 1970s colonials, where the original panels have gone brittle, and those runs get replaced in kind with backed, rigid material.

faqs.q: How is the price for a Moorestown wildlife job figured?
faqs.a: By what the inspection finds: one squirrel entry at a gable vent is a short visit, while a raccoon family plus chewed fascia and fouled insulation is several. A Moorestown slate-roof colonial with a decade-old bat colony and a Lenola cape with one squirrel entry are different universes of work, and the line-by-line quote is how that difference gets shown honestly. We walk the property with you, point out each opening, and price the removal, the sealing, and any cleanup as separate lines before work starts.

faqs.q: There is heavy thumping in my Moorestown attic at night — is it a raccoon?
faqs.a: Heavy, deliberate thumping after dark is the classic raccoon signature; squirrels sound lighter and keep daytime hours. The thumping in Moorestown usually comes from the big center-hall attics near the lake and creek, where a raccoon can raise a litter for weeks before the household hears it. We locate the entry — often a pushed-up soffit or a vent the animal has peeled back — check for a litter before anything moves, and get the family out together. Because raccoons sit on New Jersey's rabies-vector list, droppings and latrine areas in the attic get treated as contaminated material, not swept aside.

Moorestown.wildlife_intro:
Moorestown lines its Main Street with some of South Jersey's grandest older homes, then spreads into deep-lot colonials and the Lenola section's smaller postwar stock. Strawbridge Lake and the Rancocas Creek border give the town a wet, wooded frame, and the housing gives animals architecture to work with: slate and cedar roofs, stone chimneys, carriage-house conversions, and attics big enough to hold a bat colony unnoticed for years. Squirrels and raccoons are constant in the older sections; groundhogs work the creek-side and farm-edge lots to the east.

The attic is where most of the damage hides. Droppings foul insulation until it stops insulating, urine soaks ceiling drywall, and nesting shreds stored boxes and wiring jackets. A proper attic job pairs the removal itself with a cleanup decision — spot-cleaning a light mess, or pulling and replacing badly fouled insulation once the animals are out and the entries are sealed. Bat guano gets handled as a health material, bagged and carried out rather than swept dry. Homeowners see photographs of what we found, so the cleanup scope is a choice, not a surprise. Moorestown attic jobs tend to be old-colony jobs, discovered late, so cleanup scope is discussed with photographs before anyone commits to a number.

faqs.q: Do groundhogs do real damage in Willingboro?
faqs.a: They do in Burlington County: burrows under decks, sheds and foundation edges undermine slabs and channel water against the house, and garden feeding is heavy from spring through fall. Our crew traps groundhogs at active burrows and backfills and screens the site afterward.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Willingboro?
faqs.a: It depends on the animal, how many entry points your home has, and how long the animals have been inside. Our crew inspects first, explains what we found, and gives you a quote after inspection before any removal or sealing work begins, with no prices promised over the phone.

Willingboro.wildlife_intro:
Willingboro gives our crew a Burlington mix shaped by Wharton State Forest and the housing around it. The suburban northwest — Moorestown, Marlton and Mount Laurel side streets — produces steady squirrel, raccoon and mole work, while the Barrens towns around Medford and Tabernacle add groundhogs, snakes in the pines, and bats in older farmhouses and lake cabins — and Willingboro is squarely part of that pattern, with raccoons and gray squirrels in attics, skunks and opossums under decks, and seasonal bat work in the older rooflines.

Mount Holly and Burlington City keep 18th- and 19th-century brick rowhouses and Victorians, Moorestown and Medford hold historic colonials and farmhouses, and Willingboro and Marlton are postwar subdivision towns with mature trees. In fall and winter, squirrels and rodents push into warm attics and wall voids in Willingboro; spring brings denning raccoons and groundhog and skunk activity in yards, and summer is bat and mole season. Most Willingboro jobs start with a full roofline and foundation inspection, then removal and sealing of every entry we find, because closing only the obvious hole rarely holds.

faqs.q: What snakes turn up around Medford, and which are dangerous?
faqs.a: This is Pine Barrens snake country. The northern pine snake — state-Threatened, a burrower in sandy soil — is the species people meet most dramatically, and it is protected: identification and referral, never handling. A separate southern population of timber rattlesnakes also persists in the Barrens. Medford's sand roads and pine woods are prime pine snake ground, and the species' habit of hissing loudly and vibrating its tail in dry leaves convinces many homeowners they have met a rattlesnake. Common harmless residents include black racers, garter snakes, and eastern hognose, which plays dead theatrically. Non-listed snakes found inside a home can be caught and released outdoors within 200 meters.

faqs.q: What should I do about a skunk under my Medford porch?
faqs.a: Keep dogs inside after dusk and do not block the opening yourself — a skunk sealed in will spray, dig, or die under the porch, and all three are worse than the skunk. Out toward the Barrens edge, Medford skunks den under cabin steps and shed floors all winter, and the February wake-up is when most residents discover their tenants. We take skunks out with covered, low-stress handling, then trench and screen the porch perimeter with buried hardware cloth so the next one cannot move in. Skunks are a New Jersey rabies-vector species, so distance and calm are the whole technique.

Medford.wildlife_intro:
Medford is where Burlington County suburbia dissolves into the Pine Barrens. Main Street keeps a small historic village of brick and frame homes; beyond it, developments spread along Tuckerton and Stokes roads until the lots turn to pitch pine, sand, and cranberry country. Raccoons and bats work the village houses, groundhogs love the soft sandy soil at every field edge, and the Barrens fringe adds animals the suburbs rarely see: pine snakes in woodpiles, skunks under every outbuilding, and opossums in the crawlspaces of homes that back onto state forest.

On farm and acreage properties the house is only part of the job. Barns shelter raccoon families in haylofts, groundhogs undermine run-in sheds and fence lines, and skunks take up residence under equipment sheds where they are discovered by smell. We plan the property as a whole — which structures to proof, which burrows to treat, where trapping effort actually pays — instead of chasing one animal at a time. Grain and feed storage gets the same attention as the house foundation, because spilled feed is usually what drew the animals to the buildings in the first place. Medford properties often include a barn, a woodpile, and a sand driveway in the same job, and the plan covers all three because the animals use all three.

faqs.q: We keep catching rats around our Burlington City home — why do they come back?
faqs.a: Because the route and the restaurant are still open. Norway rats commute along fence lines, ivy, and utility runs, and they stay where trash, pet food, or a bird feeder feeds them every single night. In Burlington's rowhouse blocks the rat runs follow the alleys and the old fence lines, and one household sealing up while the alley stays a food route only moves the pressure next door, so we talk to the whole block when we can. We map the runs, seal the building entries in metal and mortar — rats gnaw through foam and wood — and go over the sanitation changes that make the property stop paying out. Trapping alone, without those two halves, is a subscription, not a solution.

faqs.q: Birds nest in my Burlington City bathroom vent every spring — what can be done?
faqs.a: Usually European starlings or house sparrows, the two species New Jersey's Game Code lets us deal with directly when they damage property. The nest comes out, the vent gets cleaned of the mites and debris nests carry, and a proper vent cover with a screen behind it ends the annual tenancy. High Street's older storefronts and the houses over them give starlings a row of sign cabinets and vent openings; the residential fix is the same as the commercial one: nest out, screen in, cover on. Native birds are a different matter — a chimney swift or swallow nest means timing and deterrence work only, and we will tell you honestly which bird you have before anything is touched.

Burlington City.wildlife_intro:
Burlington is one of New Jersey's oldest cities, and its housing shows it: colonial and Federal brick rowhouses on High Street, Victorians on the side streets, and a Delaware River waterfront that has been working waterfront for three centuries. Old masonry, old basements, and connected rooflines make the city rat and raccoon territory first. Rats run the riverfront blocks and the alleys between rowhouses, starlings nest in the High Street storefront signs, and raccoons work the chimneys and porch roofs of the historic districts block by block.

Crawlspaces collect problems quietly. A vent screen rusts through, a pipe penetration was never sealed, and within a season the space underneath the house holds opossums, skunks, or a raccoon latrine — along with the odor that rides the ductwork upstairs. The fix starts with a light and a full circuit underneath: every vent screened in metal, gaps around plumbing and wiring sealed, and any carcass or waste taken out. Where moisture is part of the draw, we say so plainly, because a damp crawlspace keeps attracting animals no matter how well it is screened. Burlington's old basements and crawlspaces, many of them stone or brick, get a full circuit on every job, because the voids under these houses connect in ways the street addresses do not suggest.
